title: The Tap School to the Empty Armory: Cunningham, the Coin, and the Dance About Nothing
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Centralia, the birth in the lumber town
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives 16 April 1919, Centralia, Washington. Coordinate is the city census point, the only pin the sources support
stops.campa: In a lumber and rail town of southwest Washington, between the Cascades and the coast, a son is born on the sixteenth of April to a family with no dancers in it. They name him Merce. Centralia's business is timber, sidings, and rain, and the nearest theatre worth the name stands ninety miles north in Seattle. He will spend his boyhood here and the whole of a ninety-year life elsewhere. The century he is born into has not yet settled what modern dance is, or what a man is doing on a stage that is not a vaudeville stage.
suggested_refs: Centralia, Washington, in the years of the timber boom and the Northern Pacific line

stops.name: Centralia, the tap school of Mrs. Maude Barrett
stops.date_confidence: contested and undated in the primary source. English Wikipedia attests the Barrett tap lessons but gives no year; the pool's original 1925 is unsupported; de.wikipedia says he learned tap at her school 'im Alter von 11', hence c.1930. Treat as [R]; month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: A woman named Mrs. Maude Barrett keeps a dance school in Centralia, and the boy is sent to her for tap. It is the only formal training he receives before he leaves the state. He learns the shuffle and the flap and the vaudeville steps a small Washington town still asks for, on a wooden floor, in a place with no theatre. There is no ballet here and no modern dance; there is not yet, in these years, much modern dance anywhere in America. The technique he will spend fifty years building begins in a rented room with a metal plate screwed to the toe of a shoe.
suggested_refs: Mrs. Maude Barrett's dance school, Centralia, Washington

stops.name: Seattle, the Cornish School on Capitol Hill
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month is the conventional start of the academic year and is a placeholder
stops.campa: At eighteen he crosses the state to the Cornish School on Seattle's Capitol Hill, a small conservatory where painting, music, theatre, and dance are taught in one building and the students walk between them. He arrives for theatre and stays for dance. The department teaches the Graham technique, so the contraction, the release, the fall to the floor and the weight of it reach him here two years before he sets foot in New York. He is a good student and an odd one. He is tall and quick in the feet, and he is already indifferent to whatever story a dance is supposed to be telling.
suggested_refs: Cornish College of the Arts, 710 East Roy Street, Seattle

stops.name: Seattle, the accompanist at the piano
stops.date_confidence: year attested by mercecunningham.org; month and day are placeholders. The prepared piano detail is [R], standard Cage biography, not in the fetched pool
stops.campa: Cornish keeps an accompanist for the dance classes, a Californian in his twenties who writes for percussion ensembles because the dancers need rhythm and the school cannot afford an orchestra. His name is John Cage. Within two years, in this same building, he will begin laying bolts and screws between piano strings. The two men meet across a studio floor, one counting and one playing, and open an argument about the relation of sound to movement that will run fifty-four years. The answer they arrive at is that there is no relation, and that the absence of one is the freedom.
suggested_refs: The Cornish School dance studio where Cage accompanied classes, 1938-1940

stops.name: Mills College, Oakland, Graham sees him dance
stops.date_confidence: year attested, place contested and unattested in any fetched source. Wikipedia and mercecunningham.org give no location; the pool's original 'Seattle' is unsupported; David Vaughan's standard biography places it at the Bennington School of the Dance summer session held at Mills College, Oakland, summer 1939. Vaughan was not obtainable. Month is a placeholder for the summer session
stops.campa: Martha Graham sees him dance. The Bennington summer school has moved west to Mills College for the season, and there, among students, the most powerful figure in American modern dance watches a twenty-year-old from Centralia and asks him to come to New York. He is a man, which the field is short of; he is tall and can jump, which she needs. He accepts. The whole of his training to this point is a tap school in a lumber town and two years at a conservatory on Capitol Hill, and it is enough.
sources: David Vaughan, 'Merce Cunningham: Fifty Years' (cited, not obtained)
suggested_refs: The Bennington School of the Dance summer session at Mills College, Oakland, 1939

stops.name: New York, soloist with the Martha Graham Dance Company
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month is a placeholder for the autumn season. City-centre pin: no studio address is given in the sources
stops.campa: He arrives in Manhattan and joins the Martha Graham Dance Company as a soloist, one of the first men she takes, and will dance with her six years. The city already has its dance establishments. Five years earlier George Balanchine opened the School of American Ballet on Madison Avenue; twenty-two years earlier Isadora Duncan danced the Marseillaise in red at the Metropolitan Opera. Cunningham enters neither lineage. He enters a studio where the body is made to signify, to grieve and to want, and he will spend the rest of his life taking the signifying out of it.
suggested_refs: The Martha Graham Dance Company roster, 1939-1945

stops.name: New York, the first solo concert with Cage at the piano
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by Wikipedia as April 1944; the day is not given in any fetched source and 01 is a placeholder. Venue not named in the sources; city-centre pin
stops.campa: In April he gives the first concert of his own choreography in New York, a program of solos, with John Cage at the piano playing music written for them. Cage has come east. The room is small and the audience is smaller, and this is the beginning of both the working partnership and the life the two men will share until 1992. He is still dancing for Graham by day. The dances he makes at night have no character and no story; the music does not describe them, and they do not follow the music.
suggested_refs: The April 1944 New York solo program, Cunningham's first as choreographer

stops.name: Coolidge Auditorium, Washington, the Revivalist in Appalachian Spring
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia, 'Appalachian Spring', gives the premiere as 30 October 1944 at the Coolidge Auditorium, Library of Congress, with Cunningham in the premiere cast as the Revivalist. This corrects the pool, which had tagged the claim [R] and placed it in New York
stops.campa: In the Coolidge Auditorium of the Library of Congress, Martha Graham premieres Appalachian Spring to a score commissioned from Aaron Copland. Graham dances the Bride, Erick Hawkins the Husbandman, May O'Donnell the Pioneer Woman. Cunningham dances the Revivalist, the preacher who arrives at a frontier wedding with a congregation of four women behind him and warns the couple about sin. Graham's dance takes a frontier wedding for its subject and a preacher for its antagonist. It is the last character Cunningham will ever consent to dance, the last time he stands on a stage as somebody with a name.
suggested_refs: The Coolidge Auditorium, Library of Congress, and the Copland commission of 1944

stops.name: New York, leaving Graham for the empty years
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders. The eight years of independent teaching that follow are attested only as a generality in the sources and are [R] in their detail
stops.campa: He leaves the company. There is no quarrel on record, only a divergence: Graham builds dances out of myth and psychology, and Cunningham has stopped believing a dance is about anything. He teaches, takes studio space where he can find it, and choreographs solos for himself and small pieces for whoever will rehearse. The uptown dance economy of the period runs on institutions, and George Balanchine's dancers are being sent for conditioning to Joseph Pilates's studio at 939 Eighth Avenue. Cunningham has no institution and no building. He works this way for eight years.
suggested_refs: The independent New York studio years, 1945-1953, undocumented in detail

stops.name: Black Mountain College, the summer of the Baron Medusa
stops.date_confidence: summer 1948 attested from within the corpus: buckminster_fuller.journey.json names Cage, Cunningham and de Kooning in that season, and erik_satie.journey.json carries Cage's staging of Le Piege de Meduse with Fuller as the Baron. Month is a placeholder for the summer session. Cunningham as the mechanical monkey is [R]
stops.campa: Josef Albers calls Cage and Cunningham to Black Mountain College for the summer session, onto a campus that also holds Willem de Kooning and Buckminster Fuller. Cage mounts Erik Satie's little play Le Piege de Meduse and casts Fuller, who has never acted, as the Baron Medusa; Cunningham dances the mechanical monkey. Fuller raises his first geodesic dome here out of venetian-blind strips and it folds to the ground. Anni Albers is weaving in the same buildings. The college has almost no money and this summer has Cage, Cunningham, Fuller, de Kooning and the Alberses on one hillside at one time.
suggested_refs: The Black Mountain College summer session of 1948 and the collapsed supine dome

stops.name: Urbana, Illinois, Suite by Chance
stops.date_confidence: attested; mercecunningham.org gives the premiere as 24 March 1953 at the University of Illinois, Urbana. This corrects the pool, which credited the premiere to a company that did not yet exist and gave the place as 'USA'. Christian Wolff's score is [R]
stops.campa: At the University of Illinois in Urbana, on the twenty-fourth of March, he premieres Suite by Chance, the first work built entirely by throwing for it. The movements, their order, their duration and their place on the stage are each decided by charts and coin tosses rather than by his preference. Christian Wolff supplies an electronic score. What Cage has found in the I Ching in these years, Cunningham takes into the body, where it is harder, because a leg cannot be indeterminate. A leg must go somewhere. The chance decides where; the dancer then does it exactly.
stops.quote: John Cage and I became interested in the use of chance in the 50s. I think one of the very primary things that happened then was the publication of the 'I Ching', the Chinese book of changes, from which you can cast your fortune: the hexagrams.
stops.quote_source: Merce Cunningham, in 'Merce Cunningham: A Lifetime of Dance', dir. Charles Atlas, documentary film, 2000; transcribed at Wikipedia, 'Merce Cunningham', section 'Chance operations'. Wikiquote miscites this as a book; no timecode exists
suggested_refs: Suite by Chance, University of Illinois, Urbana, 24 March 1953

stops.name: Black Mountain College, the company is formed
stops.date_confidence: year and place attested by Wikipedia and mercecunningham.org; month is a placeholder for the summer residency. The founding roster named here is [R], standard, not in the fetched pool
stops.campa: He returns to Black Mountain for the summer and makes a company out of the dancers in his class: Carolyn Brown, Viola Farber, Remy Charlip, Paul Taylor among the first of them. Cage is music director. Robert Rauschenberg, who has been at the college himself, will design the sets, lights and costumes from the following year and for a decade after. The company has no theatre, no season and no subscribers, and it will tour in a Volkswagen bus. It gives its dancers the one thing the New York dance economy cannot: work made without anyone asking what the work is for.
stops.quote: I was working on a title called, 'Untitled Solo', and I had made—using the chance operations—a series of movements written on scraps of paper for the legs and the arms, the head, all different. And it was done not to the music but with the music of Christian Wolff.
stops.quote_source: Merce Cunningham, in 'Merce Cunningham: A Lifetime of Dance', dir. Charles Atlas, 2000; transcribed at Wikipedia, 'Merce Cunningham'. Quoted whole and alone: the circulating version splices it to a sentence from a different paragraph
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Merce Cunningham Dance Company' (Rauschenberg resident designer 1954-1964)
suggested_refs: The founding roster of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company, Black Mountain College, summer 1953

stops.name: New York, Suite for Five and the two fellowships
stops.date_confidence: year attested by mercecunningham.org; month, day and place are not given, the pool records only 'USA', and the pin is a city-centre placeholder. The paper-imperfection method is [R]. The Guggenheim Fellowships of 1954 and 1959 are attested by Wikipedia
stops.campa: He makes Suite for Five, taking its structure from the imperfections in a sheet of paper: he marks where the flaws fall and reads them as positions in space and moments in time. Cage's Music for Piano is composed the same way, from the same kind of blemish. A Guggenheim Fellowship two years earlier has bought some of the time, and a second will come in 1959. The company is poor and the work is exacting. He has already set his position down in print, in an essay about the impermanence of the art he practises.
stops.quote: If a dancer dances--which is not the same as having theories about dancing or wishing to dance or trying to dance or remembering in his body someone else's dance--but if the dancer dances, everything is there. ... Our ecstasy in dance comes from the possible gift of freedom, the exhilarating moment that this exposing of the bare energy can give us. What is meant is not license, but freedom, that is, a complete awareness of the world and at the same time a detachment from it.
stops.quote_source: Merce Cunningham, 'The Impermanent Art', 7 Arts No. 3, pp. 69-77, Falcon's Wing Press, Colorado, 1955; full text at mercecunningham.org. The two passages are separated by roughly four paragraphs and the ellipsis marks the cut. Commonly and wrongly circulated as a 1952 statement
suggested_refs: Suite for Five (1956) and the sheet of flawed paper that generated it

segments.name: Events, the Walker, and the World

stops.name: New York, Crises and the elastic bands
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for both Crises and the Dance Magazine Award, and 1959 for the second Guggenheim; month, day and venue are unrecorded in the sources and the pin is a city-centre placeholder
stops.campa: He premieres Crises, in which the dancers are bound to one another by elastic bands at the wrist and the waist, so that a step taken by one is felt as a pull by another. It is the closest his work comes to depicting a relation between two people, and it does it mechanically, with rubber. Dance Magazine gives him its award the same year, and a second Guggenheim Fellowship had arrived the year before. He is forty-one. The company is seven years old, has never had a home, and rehearses wherever a floor can be borrowed.
suggested_refs: Crises (1960), the elastic-band constraint

stops.name: Minneapolis, the Walker Art Center opens its floor
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for the first Walker performance and for Field Dances and Story; months and days are unrecorded. The Walker pin is the museum's own coordinate
stops.campa: The company dances at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis for the first time and begins a relationship with that museum which will run twenty-five years. A museum, not a theatre. The same year he premieres Field Dances, in which the dancers are handed material and left to choose what to do with it and when to stop, and Story, whose set and costumes are assembled from whatever Robert Rauschenberg finds backstage that night: a sweater, a crate, a coat. No two performances of Story are alike, and nobody, the choreographer included, ever sees it twice.
suggested_refs: The Walker Art Center's twenty-five-year Cunningham relationship, from 1963

stops.name: Pocket Theatre, Third Avenue, the eight hundred and forty repetitions
stops.date_confidence: attested from within the corpus via erik_satie.journey.json. Cunningham's own presence in the theatre is not attested anywhere and is not claimed here
stops.campa: On the ninth of September, in a small house on Third Avenue, Cage mounts the first complete performance of Erik Satie's Vexations, a single page the composer marked to be repeated eight hundred and forty times. It runs eighteen hours and forty minutes. A relay of pianists spell one another at the keyboard, David Tudor and Christian Wolff and John Cale and Joshua Rifkin among them. Cunningham's music director has spent a day and a night establishing that duration by itself can be a form, and the audience thins and returns through the night.
sources: erik_satie.journey.json (stop: 'New York, Cage plays Vexations through')
suggested_refs: The Pocket Theatre relay of Satie's Vexations, 9-10 September 1963

stops.name: New York, the Cunningham Dance Foundation is incorporated
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders; no address is given in the sources
stops.campa: A foundation is incorporated to carry the company: to raise the money, hold the contracts, pay the dancers something, and keep the enterprise breathing between engagements. It is the first institutional body Cunningham has ever had, twenty-five years after he arrived in the city and eleven years after the company was made at Black Mountain. It will outlive him by less than three years. Its final act, in 2012, will be to dissolve itself in his own studio and hand everything he made to a trust.
suggested_refs: The Cunningham Dance Foundation, 1964-2012

stops.name: Paris, the six-month world tour crosses Europe
stops.date_confidence: the 1964 six-month world tour is attested by Wikipedia, which gives the place only as 'multiple countries'. The itinerary named in this campa is [R]. Coordinate is the canonical Paris city pin inherited byte-identical from erik_satie, isadora_duncan and laban
stops.campa: The company leaves for six months and comes back a different animal. It is the first time Cunningham's work is seen outside the United States, and Europe takes it as America has not: as the arrival of something finished rather than the experiment of a difficult man. The route runs through Western and Eastern Europe, India, Thailand and Japan, by bus and by train, with Rauschenberg travelling as lighting designer and stage manager and painting in the theatres between shows. In Paris the house is loud in both directions at once. Paris will be the company's second city for forty years.
suggested_refs: The 1964 six-month world tour of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company

stops.name: Vienna, Museum Event No. 1
stops.date_confidence: date and place rest on standard Cunningham literature and not on a re-fetchable source: the Merce Cunningham Trust's Events page returned HTTP 404 on the verification pass. What is established is that the pool's original 'USA' is unsupported and collides with the world tour running that month. Treat the location as [R]
stops.campa: In the Museum des 20. Jahrhunderts, on the twenty-fourth of June, the company performs the first of what will be called Events: not a program of dances but a continuous ninety minutes assembled out of fragments of the repertory and fitted to whatever room it is given. There is no proscenium, no curtain, no interval and no front. The audience stands or sits where it can and sees a different set of simultaneities depending on where it happens to be standing. He will make hundreds of these over forty-five years, in gymnasiums, galleries, plazas and drill halls.
sources: Merce Cunningham Trust Events page (HTTP 404, not reachable)
suggested_refs: Museum Event No. 1, Museum des 20. Jahrhunderts, Vienna, 24 June 1964

stops.name: New York, Changes and the silver clouds of RainForest
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for both the book and RainForest; months, days and venue are unrecorded and the pin is a city-centre placeholder. Jasper Johns's role as artistic adviser in this period is [R]
stops.campa: He publishes Changes: Notes on Choreography, a book laid out as loosely as its subject, pages of chance charts and rehearsal notes and photographs set down without an argument to connect them. The same year he premieres RainForest, danced among Andy Warhol's Silver Clouds, helium pillows of metallised plastic that drift where the dancers' passage pushes them and have to be weighted so they will not leave the stage. Jasper Johns is close to the company by now. The set will not hold still, and it is not asked to.
stops.quote: Merce is my favorite artist in any field. Sometimes I'm pleased by the complexity of a work I paint. By the fourth day I realize it's simple. Nothing Merce does is simple. Everything has a fascinating richness and multiplicity of direction.
stops.quote_source: Jasper Johns, quoted in Hubert Saal, 'Merce', Newsweek 71, no. 22, 27 May 1968, p. 88; reprinted in Varnedoe (ed.), 'Jasper Johns: Writings, Sketchbook Notes, Interviews', MoMA 1996, p. 129; text as given by Tate In Focus, 'Johns and Cunningham'. The circulating trim drops the last clause
suggested_refs: RainForest (1968) with Andy Warhol's Silver Clouds; Changes: Notes on Choreography (1968)

stops.name: New York, Canfield dealt from a deck
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for Canfield and 1970 for Second Hand; months, days and venues are unrecorded. Pauline Oliveros's score, the Socrate basis of Second Hand and the copyright refusal behind Cheap Imitation are all [R], standard, not in the fetched pool
stops.campa: He premieres Canfield, whose structure is dealt from a deck of playing cards, the solitaire game of that name deciding which parts are performed and in what order on a given night. Pauline Oliveros writes the score. A vertical bar of light crosses the stage all evening, scanning it. The following year he makes Second Hand, which begins in Erik Satie's Socrate and ends in music Cage has had to rewrite from scratch because the publisher refused permission. The refusal becomes the piece, and Cage gives it the title Cheap Imitation.
suggested_refs: Canfield (1969) and Second Hand (1970), with Cage's Cheap Imitation

stops.name: Westbeth, the studio above the Hudson
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders. Coordinate is the Westbeth Artists Community pin used in the research pool's afterlife section
stops.campa: The company takes studios on the top floor of Westbeth, the old Bell Telephone Laboratories on the Hudson at Bethune Street, converted into subsidised housing and workspace for artists. After eighteen years the work has an address. There is a sprung floor, windows over the river, and a school attached that will teach the Cunningham technique for four decades. Everything after this is made here: the notation, the video experiments, the computer work, and the last solos of a man who by the end cannot stand up without help.
suggested_refs: The Westbeth Artists Community studio, 55 Bethune Street, from 1971

stops.name: 107 Bank Street, the shared apartment
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. No source fetched this pass attests either address: Wikipedia's Cage and Cunningham articles mention neither 107 Bank Street nor 101 West 18th Street. The pool's claim of 'decades' at Bank Street is an overstatement; tradition gives roughly 1971 to 1979. The pool's coordinate sat about 100 m off and has been corrected here
stops.campa: Cage and Cunningham live together in the West Village, a few streets from the studio, in rooms full of plants and stones and Cage's manuscripts. They have been a couple for a quarter of a century and have said nothing public about it; the arrangement is known to everyone in the field and printed by nobody. At the end of the decade they will move to a loft on West Eighteenth Street. Cunningham will live there alone for thirty years after Cage's death, and he will die in it.
suggested_refs: 107 Bank Street and the later loft at 101 West 18th Street, both unsourced in reachable material

stops.name: New York, Sounddance and the turn to the camera
stops.date_confidence: Sounddance is attested to 1975 and the Capezio Award to 1977 by Wikipedia; the turn to film and video is tagged [R] in the pool and dated only to the mid-1970s. Months, days and venues unrecorded; city-centre pin. Charles Atlas as collaborating filmmaker is [R]
stops.campa: He premieres Sounddance, ten minutes of speed for six dancers who enter one at a time through a slit in a draped backdrop and are finally expelled through the same slit, to David Tudor's Toneburst. In these years he also turns to the camera, making dances for film and video rather than filming dances made for the stage: the frame becomes another kind of stage, with its own front, its own distances and no audience to be seated correctly. Charles Atlas works the camera. The Capezio Award comes in 1977 and the Scripps in 1982.
suggested_refs: Sounddance (1975); the video works made with Charles Atlas from the mid-1970s

stops.name: Minskoff Theatre, Broadway, Rauschenberg returns for Travelogue
stops.date_confidence: attested; mercecunningham.org gives the premiere as 18 January 1977 at the Minskoff Theatre, New York, with Cage's Telephones and Birds
stops.campa: Robert Rauschenberg comes back. He had been the company's resident designer from 1954 through the world tour of 1964 and had not worked with Cunningham or Cage since. For Travelogue he makes a set of bicycle wheels, ladders and long bolts of coloured cloth; Cage supplies Telephones and Birds. Thirteen years of separation close in a single evening on Forty-fifth Street. The three of them will work together again intermittently until Rauschenberg's death, and the last of those collaborations is thirty years off.
stops.quote: Rauschenberg's first collaboration with Cunningham and Cage since 1964.
stops.quote_source: Merce Cunningham Trust, mercecunningham.org, choreography page for Travelogue (1977)
suggested_refs: Travelogue, Minskoff Theatre, 18 January 1977

stops.name: Washington, the Kennedy Center and the MacArthur in one year
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for both honours; the Kennedy Center Honors are held in December but no month is given in the fetched sources, so 01-01 is a placeholder. Coordinate is the Kennedy Center
stops.campa: In one year the American state and its largest private foundation both decide that he is a national possession. He is named a Kennedy Center Honoree, and the MacArthur Foundation gives him a fellowship with no conditions attached to it at all. He is sixty-six. He has been making dances for forty-one years, most of them to half-empty houses, and the Samuel H. Scripps American Dance Festival Award had reached him three years before. The money goes into the company, which still tours in whatever vehicle it can afford.
suggested_refs: The 1985 Kennedy Center Honors class; the MacArthur Fellowship of 1985

stops.name: London, the Olivier Award
stops.date_confidence: year attested by mercecunningham.org; month and day are placeholders and the pin is the London city centre. The characterisation of the company's European reception in this campa is [R]
stops.campa: The Laurence Olivier Award, given in London for the year's outstanding achievement in dance, goes to Cunningham in the same twelvemonth as the Kennedy Center and the MacArthur. Britain had been slower than France to take him and quicker than his own country. The company has been crossing Europe for twenty-one years by this point, and there are seasons in London and Paris where the house is full and the reception is closer to that given a returning composer than to that given a visiting dance troupe.
suggested_refs: The 1985 Laurence Olivier Award for dance

stops.name: Paris, Chevalier of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders. Coordinate is the canonical Paris city pin inherited byte-identical from erik_satie, isadora_duncan and laban
stops.campa: France makes him a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour, and will raise him to Officier fifteen years later. This is the republic that gave Isadora Duncan her audiences and let Rudolf Laban pass a destitute winter in Paris in 1937 on his way out of Germany, and whose notation systems the dance world still uses to write down what Cunningham's coins decide. Paris has been the company's second city since the world tour: the theatres are willing, the critics write about the work rather than around it, and the chance procedures are not received as a provocation.
suggested_refs: The 1989 grade of Chevalier in the Ordre national de la Legion d'honneur

stops.name: Washington, the National Medal of Arts
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month, day and ceremony venue are unrecorded and the pin is the White House as the conventional site of the award
stops.campa: The United States gives him the National Medal of Arts. The dances that were walked out of in the fifties are on the syllabus now, and the conservatories that once refused the technique teach it. Chance operations have stopped being a scandal and become a method. He is seventy-one. Cage is seventy-seven and has two years to live. The company is thirty-seven years old and still travelling, and Cunningham still teaches the morning class himself whenever he is in New York.
suggested_refs: The 1990 National Medal of Arts

stops.name: New York, LifeForms and the body that cannot tire
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders. That LifeForms came out of Simon Fraser University is [R], not in the fetched pool
stops.campa: He begins choreographing with LifeForms, a computer animation program built at a Canadian university, assembling phrases on a screen figure that has no fear, no fatigue and no sense of what a human body will refuse to do. The program proposes transitions he would never have thought of and some the dancers cannot execute; he keeps the ones they can. He is seventy-two, his knees are finished, and he has found a way to go on inventing movement he can no longer demonstrate. After this the dances get harder, not easier.
suggested_refs: The LifeForms animation software and the choreography made in it from 1991

stops.name: Greenwich Village, the death of John Cage
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives the stroke and the death on 12 August 1992 in Manhattan. The coordinate is St. Vincent's Hospital, Greenwich Village, named in the research pool. That Cunningham cancelled no engagements is [R]
stops.campa: John Cage suffers a stroke in the loft on West Eighteenth Street and dies at St. Vincent's Hospital in Greenwich Village. He is seventy-nine. The two men had met across a studio floor at the Cornish School fifty-four years earlier and had not been apart for long since: accompanist, then composer, then music director, then housemate, and always the other half of a single proposition, that music and dance should be made separately and meet only in performance. Cunningham cancels nothing. The autumn touring goes forward and he dances in it.
suggested_refs: St. Vincent's Hospital, Greenwich Village, 12 August 1992

stops.name: Stony Point, the ashes in the Ramapo Mountains
stops.date_confidence: the scattering is attested by Wikipedia; its date is not recorded anywhere reachable, and 1992-09-01 is a placeholder set after the August death. Coordinate as given in the research pool
stops.campa: Cage's ashes are scattered in the Ramapo Mountains near Stony Point, north of the city, at the place where he had earlier scattered his parents'. The two of them had lived at the Gate Hill cooperative there in the fifties, among the potters and the composers, before the loft years. There is no stone. When Cunningham's own turn comes seventeen years later he will leave no grave either, and no accessible source records what becomes of his remains. Two of the most documented artists of the century leave nothing behind that can be visited.
sources: research pool, afterlife section (no grave recorded for Cunningham)
suggested_refs: The Gate Hill Cooperative, Stony Point, New York, and the Ramapo scattering

stops.name: New York and Saratoga Springs, CRWDSPCR and the hall of fame
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for both CRWDSPCR and the induction; months and days are unrecorded. Coordinate is the National Museum of Dance, Saratoga Springs; CRWDSPCR's own premiere venue is not given in the sources
stops.campa: He premieres CRWDSPCR, made entirely in LifeForms, its title readable as crowd spacer or as crowd's pacer, the vowels stripped out the way a file name strips them. The dancers move at different tempi in the same space with nobody leading. The same year the National Museum of Dance at Saratoga Springs puts him in its hall of fame, which is one way of saying that the field he spent fifty years declining to join has decided that he founded it. He is seventy-four and still teaching the company class.

stops.name: Cirque Royal, Brussels, Ocean in the round
stops.date_confidence: attested; mercecunningham.org gives the premiere as 18 May 1994 at the Cirque Royal, Brussels, with music by Andrew Culver and David Tudor and design by Marsha Skinner. This corrects the pool, which gave the place as 'USA'. The figure of 112 musicians is [R]
stops.campa: At the Cirque Royal in Brussels, in a ring with the audience all around it and the musicians ranged above, the company dances Ocean. Cage had drawn the concept up in 1991, a dance in a circular space with the spectators surrounding the dancers, and died before it could be made. Andrew Culver composes Ocean 1-95 to the plan, David Tudor supplies Soundings: Ocean Diary, Marsha Skinner designs it. Ninety minutes, no front, no back, and a dead collaborator's instruction carried out to the letter three years after he stopped being able to check.
stops.quote: John Cage's original concept of Ocean, in 1991, was for a dance to be performed in a circular space, with the audience surrounding the dancers.
stops.quote_source: Merce Cunningham Trust, mercecunningham.org, choreography page for Ocean (1994)

stops.name: New York, Hand-drawn Spaces and the projected dancers of BIPED
stops.date_confidence: years attested by Wikipedia, 1998 for Hand-drawn Spaces and 1999 for BIPED; places given only as 'USA'. BIPED's premiere is commonly placed at Zellerbach Hall, Berkeley, which was not verifiable this pass, so a city-centre placeholder pin is used. Paul Kaiser and Shelley Eshkar as collaborators are corroborated by openendedgroup.com
stops.campa: With Paul Kaiser and Shelley Eshkar he makes Hand-drawn Spaces, an animated work with no dancers in it: motion capture lifts the movement off living bodies and hangs it on hand-drawn figures that walk out of the dark. The following year the method returns to the stage in BIPED, where projected figures of light cross a scrim in front of the living company at the same scale, performing the same phrases. He is eighty. The dancers share the floor with recordings of dancers, and nobody in the house is told which is which.

stops.name: New York State Theater, dancing at eighty with Baryshnikov
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives the date and the venue. The description of Cunningham's physical condition on the night is [R]
stops.campa: For his eightieth birthday the company gives a program at the New York State Theater at Lincoln Center, and Mikhail Baryshnikov dances in it with him. Baryshnikov had left the Kirov, then American Ballet Theatre, and had spent the nineties working through choreographers his training never prepared him for; Cunningham's is the hardest of them. The two of them appear together on a stage built for George Balanchine's company. Cunningham can barely walk. He moves his arms and his head, and the house comes to its feet.

stops.name: Paris, Officier of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders. Coordinate is the canonical Paris city pin inherited byte-identical from erik_satie, isadora_duncan and laban
stops.campa: France raises him to Officier of the Legion of Honour, fifteen years after the Chevalier's cross. He is eighty-five. The company still tours, still opens with an Event in whatever room the presenter can give it, and still travels with its own floor rolled in the truck. The dances of this last decade are made on a screen in the morning and taught to the dancers in the afternoon, by a man sitting in a chair at the front of the studio and marking with his hands what his legs gave up doing years ago. Of the Black Mountain summer, Cage and de Kooning and Fuller are dead; Rauschenberg is in Florida; Cunningham is on the road.

stops.name: Tokyo, the Praemium Imperiale
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day are placeholders, and no source reached says whether Cunningham travelled to receive it. Coordinate is the Tokyo city centre
stops.campa: The Japan Art Association gives him the Praemium Imperiale, an award made in the name of a prince and treated across the arts as the prize the Nobel committee never got around to instituting. He is eighty-six and has been making dances for sixty-one years. Japan had taken the company on the world tour of 1964, and the Events had needed no explaining there: a form with no front, assembled for whatever room it is given and watched from wherever a body happens to be standing, is not received there as a foreign proposition.

stops.name: New York, XOVER and the opening of Loops
stops.date_confidence: XOVER is attested to 2007 by Wikipedia; venue unrecorded and the pin is a city-centre placeholder. stops.campa: He premieres XOVER, with a decor drawn from a Rauschenberg painting and a score by Cage; it is the last work the two of them make together, and Rauschenberg dies the following May. In the same season the OpenEnded Group, who built the motion capture for BIPED, reopen Loops. The hand-motion data recorded from Cunningham's arthritic fingers, and the code that renders it into moving line, are put out as open source under a Mellon grant. Not the choreography, which is a solo of 1971. The hands themselves become a file that anyone can run.

stops.name: Brooklyn Academy of Music, Nearly Ninety and the Legacy Plan
stops.date_confidence: the premiere is attested by Wikipedia and timed to his ninetieth birthday, 16 April 2009; the Legacy Plan announcement is attested to June 2009 and is described in the same campa. Benedetta Tagliabue's set and the rock score are [R]
stops.campa: On his ninetieth birthday the company premieres Nearly Ninety at the Brooklyn Academy of Music: two hours, a set by Benedetta Tagliabue, a rock score, and Cunningham watching from a wheelchair in the wings. Two months later the foundation makes public the Legacy Plan, drawn up with him while he is alive: a final two-year world tour, a complete filmed record of the repertory, a documented capsule for every work, the creation of a trust to license future stagings, and then the dissolution of the company. He has arranged his own posthumous affairs the way he arranged a dance, in advance and by rule.

stops.name: New York, death in the loft
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives death at his home in New York City on 26 July 2009, aged 90. The specific address is not attested in anything reachable, so the city pin from the research pool is used rather than the traditional West Eighteenth Street loft
stops.campa: He dies at home in Manhattan, three months past ninety, ten weeks after the Legacy Plan was made public and three months after Nearly Ninety. There is no funeral of state and no grave; no accessible source records what is done with his body. The company he made out of a summer class at Black Mountain has fifty-six years behind it and two years and five months ahead of it, and every one of those months is already booked. The dances will go on being performed for exactly as long as he decided, and then they will stop.

stops.name: Park Avenue Armory, the last night of the company
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives the final performance as 31 December 2011 at the Park Avenue Armory. That the evening took the form of Events in the drill hall is [R]
stops.campa: On the last night of the year the Merce Cunningham Dance Company dances for the last time, in the drill hall of the Park Avenue Armory, the audience moving around a floor that has no front. The two-year farewell tour of the Legacy Plan ends here. At midnight the dancers stop, and a company that has given close to three thousand performances in more than forty countries ceases to exist, by a decision its founder took while he was alive to take it. The dissolution is not a failure of funding. It is the last piece of choreography.

stops.name: Westbeth, the foundation dissolves itself
stops.date_confidence: attested; mercecunningham.org and Wikipedia give the final board meeting as 15 March 2012, in the Westbeth studio, with assets transferring to the Merce Cunningham Trust
stops.campa: The board of the Cunningham Dance Foundation meets for the last time in the studio at Westbeth, forty-one years after the company moved in, and votes itself out of existence. The assets pass to the Merce Cunningham Trust, which takes offices at 130 West 56th Street and will license the technique classes, the teacher training, and the staged reconstructions of RainForest and Summerspace and Fabrications by dancers who learned them from him. The floor is rolled up and the school closes, forty-eight years after the foundation was incorporated to keep the company alive.
